1.pericope_label: Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not; But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.

schools.summary: Identify the ministry referred to as the one just described, of the new covenant, of the Spirit, of righteousness and of glory, and note the two thoughts that rise with it: the writer's own unworthiness, expressed in the words about having received mercy, and the trials in the midst of which the work had to be done — the calling itself being the reason he cannot faint or show cowardice. Give the verb its force: it means to behave badly under pressure, to give in to evil, to lose courage, and the man it describes is the faint-hearted coward. Then take the renouncing at its root, a verb meaning to speak off or away from, found nowhere else in these writings, and set the renunciation against the religions of the nations, which were largely trick and were maintained by deceiving the ignorant; draw the rule that truth never needs such arts, that no cause long succeeds by cunning, and that religion is open and straightforward, having no alliance with artifice. On the phrase rendered hidden things of dishonesty, prefer hidden things of shame, and observe that the English word once bore a wider sense than it does now; but hold that the context points not to sensual vice, nor to dishonesty in the modern meaning, but to subtlety and underhand dealing, and reconstruct the dilemma the opponents had built — either the change of plan showed a discreditable fickleness, or something worse than fickleness. Trace the two remaining terms to their roots, the one meaning a doer of any deed whatever and so a clever or unscrupulous man, the other from a word for bait, used of adulterating gold or wine, and nearly equivalent to the corrupting spoken of earlier. Close on the appeal: it is made not to men's tastes or prejudices or humours but to the highest thing in them, their conscience.

Explain what the ministers did and did not do. They did not sink in spirit or give out from the work under reproaches and persecutions, being encouraged by the excellence of the ministry itself, which was valuable in its nature and useful in its effects; and they behaved so that they were the same men in public as in private, using no art to cover either their doctrine or their lives, whereas the false teachers took pains to colour over both their sentiments and their conduct. Then set out the ground of it: the writer returns to a commendation of himself personally, having digressed into the dignity of the gospel in general, and shows that what he preaches is that gospel. He premises that he had not reached such a pinnacle of honour by his own efforts or merits but had been led forward by the mercy of God alone — and note that grounding the apostleship in God's mercy implies more than grounding it in his grace. Gloss the denial of fainting by what it means in practice, that we are not deficient in our duty and omit nothing of what belongs to our office. On the hidden things, canvass the readings offered by others, that the shadows of the Mosaic law are meant, or the vain show by which the false teachers recommended themselves, and take instead a third: the phrase covers all the disguises with which they adulterated the pure and native beauty of the gospel. Support it with the comparison that decides it — chaste and virtuous women, satisfied with the gracefulness of natural beauty, do not resort to artificial adorning, while harlots never think themselves adorned enough until nature has been corrupted; so the apostle glories in having set forth the pure gospel while others set forth one disguised and covered over with unseemly additions, framing a new gospel not unlike a profane philosophy, swelled with empty bombast and devoid of the efficacy of the Spirit.

Report the textual variant before the exposition, since some copies read not we faint not but we act not wickedly, a reading supported by several uncials and thought genuine by one editor, and one which joins smoothly to the clause that follows: as we have been graciously entrusted with this ministry, we do not act wickedly, but have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty. Then say what the renouncing covers. It is the hidden things of shame, the things wicked men do and are ashamed to have known; and one authority refers it to carnal abominations, there having been people at Corinth who taught that fornication was no sin. Take the next term as subtlety and clever cunning, the word being compounded of the words for all and for work, and the one after it as using the doctrines of the gospel to serve a secular or carnal purpose, explaining away their force to palliate sin, or generalising the precepts so that particular circumstances excuse obedience. Then bring it home, since there are deceitful handlers of this kind still in the garb of Christian ministers: men who disguise the part of their creed that would make them unpopular, who affect moderation in order to procure a larger audience and wider support, who leave the prevalent and popular vices unattacked, who call dissipation of mind relaxation and worldly pleasures innocent amusements — in a word, who turn with the tide and shift with the wind of popular opinion, prejudice and fashion. Sum the whole of it as adding to the word, altering it, or accommodating it to the taste of the hearers; and say what the ministry itself means, that we desist not in any degree from our glorious enterprise, having been mercifully supported in all our trials.

Take the chapter as a vindication of the ministry against false teachers who called its ministers deceitful workers, or tried to prejudice the people against them on account of their sufferings. Observe first what the dignity of the office did not produce: they were not puffed up with pride, did not take state upon themselves, and did not indulge in idleness, but were spurred on to greater diligence, so that being distinguished and dignified they were the more excited to the performance of their duty. Then observe their constancy: they did not faint under the difficulty of the work nor desist from the labour, and their steadfastness is expressly traced to the mercy of God, since from the same mercy and grace by which they received the apostleship they received strength to persevere in the work of that office. Draw the note that follows from it: as it is great mercy and grace to be called to be saints, so it is a special mercy to be counted faithful and to be put into the ministry.

Hear a deliberate lowering of the voice at this point. Having uttered great things, and having set himself and all the faithful before Moses, and being aware of the height and greatness of what he had said, observe how he moderates his tone again. It was necessary on account of the false Apostles both to exalt his hearers and to calm down that swelling — yet not to do away with it altogether, since that would be a trifler's part. So he manages it another way, by showing that it was not of their own merits but all of the loving-kindness of God: nothing more did they contribute except that they became ministers and made themselves subservient to the things given by God, which is why the word used is not largess, nor supply, but ministry. Nor is he content even with that, but adds the words about having obtained mercy, since the very ministering to these things is of mercy and loving-kindness. Press the point further, for it belongs to mercy to deliver from evils, not to give so many good things besides — and yet the mercy of God includes this also. Take the clause about mercy as governing both the ministry and the not fainting, and observe throughout how earnestly he endeavours to lower his own things.

debates.question: What are the hidden things of shame?

sides.position: Carnal abominations; there were people at Corinth who taught that fornication was no sin
Not sensual vice, nor dishonesty in the modern sense, but subtlety and underhand dealing
Every disguise by which the gospel was adulterated — the harlot's paint against the chaste woman's natural beauty
Everything scandalous to the gospel in doctrine or practice, so that they were the same men in public as in private

debates.question: Does the verse read we faint not or we act not wickedly?

sides.position: Several uncials give we act not wickedly, thought genuine by one editor, and it joins smoothly to what follows
The verb means to behave badly under pressure and so to lose courage; the man described is the faint-hearted coward

debates.question: Why is the ministry grounded in mercy rather than merit?

sides.position: Nothing was contributed but that they became ministers; the very ministering is of mercy and loving-kindness
Grounding the apostleship in God's mercy implies more than grounding it in his grace
From the same mercy by which they received the office they received strength to persevere in it

outliers.note: Alone carries the charge of handling the word deceitfully into his own century, naming the practices — softening an unpopular article, affecting moderation for a larger audience, leaving fashionable vices alone, calling dissipation relaxation.
Alone reads the opening as a deliberate management of tone, in which the writer must both raise his hearers and bring down the swelling he has caused, without doing away with it altogether.

themes: seeing we have this ministry, we faint not
renounced the hidden things of dishonesty
commending ourselves to every man's conscience

3.pericope_label: But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.

schools.summary: Concede the fact and deny the inference. It cannot be denied that the beauty and glory of the gospel were not perceived by many, notwithstanding the plainness with which its truths were made known; but that is not to be traced to any want of clearness in the gospel itself, nor to any purpose of God to conceal its meaning. Hear in the language a deliberate allusion to the veil the lawgiver put on his own face, and turn it round: there is a veil here too, but it lies on the hearers. Correct two words to keep the sequence: it has been veiled rather than is hid, and among them that are perishing rather than them that are lost; and note carefully that the present participle does not exclude the thought of future change. Widen the class as well, against those who confine it to Judaising teachers, to the whole body of those who are at present on the way to perish, not knowing God and counting themselves unworthy of eternal life. On the phrase that follows, admit that the title sounds startling as a description of the devil but set beside it the prince of this world and the prince of the power of the air; the world that lies in wickedness worships the spirit of hate and falsehood and selfishness, and in doing so practically deifies him. Note that the name god is given not because he has any divine attribute but because he actually receives the homage of the men of this world, as an idol does. Give the tense its value, an act in past time rather than a continuing state, and observe that the noun for the unbelieving is used with special reference to the outside heathen world, whose spiritual state was lower than Israel's: the veil lay over the heart of the one, while in the other the very organs of spiritual perception were blinded. Then state the mechanism plainly: they refused to believe, and so the blinding followed, which is what happens with wilful disbelievers.

Meet the objection first. It might have been easy to pour calumny on what had been said about the clearness of his preaching, since he had many adversaries; and the answer given is stern, for he threatens all who do not acknowledge the power of his gospel and warns them that their blindness is a token of reprobation. Anyone affirming that he does not perceive that manifestation shows himself by that very token to be blind and destitute of understanding, for the sincerity of the teaching is clearly perceived by all who have eyes; and add the image that settles it, that the sun is not less resplendent because the blind do not perceive his light. Then answer the question of who is meant by the god of this world, and answer it without hesitation: no one who judges rightly can doubt that it is Satan. Explain the title so that it grants him nothing, since it is owed not to any hand in making the world or any concern in governing it, but to his influence over the worst and greatest part of it, which lies in wickedness under his power, led captive at his will and doing his lusts. Then give the history of the other reading and be candid about it. Hilary, having to do with Arians who abused this passage to deny Christ's true divinity, twisted the text into a statement that God had blinded the understandings of this world; Chrysostom afterwards followed him, with the view of not conceding to the Manicheans their two principles; Augustine had the same reason, having to contend with the same people, while what influenced Ambrose does not appear. Draw the moral from the method rather than the men: we see what the heat of controversy does in carrying on disputes, for had all those men calmly read the words it would never have occurred to any of them to twist them into a forced meaning; but being harassed by opponents, they were more concerned to refute them than to investigate what was actually meant.

Read the veil as lying only on the wilfully blind, and take the word for the lost in its wider sense: it does not necessarily mean those who will perish eternally but is a common epithet for a man without the gospel and without God in the world, the very sort whom Christ came to seek and to save — as when the disciples were sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and when the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost. Then enter a dissent on the title. Own a considerable reluctance to assign the epithet the God to Satan, and say that were there not a rooted prejudice in favour of the common opinion the contrary might be well vindicated, namely that by the God of this world the supreme Being is meant, who in his judgment gave over the minds of the unbelieving to spiritual darkness so that destruction came upon them to the uttermost. Support it by noting that although Satan has claimed the kingdoms of the world and their glory as his to give, God has nowhere said so. Observe also the order of cause and effect in the verse, that those whose minds are blinded are they who believe not, and that because they believe not their minds continue in darkness and become proper subjects for the adversary to work upon, who then deepens the darkness and increases the hardness. On the last clause, call the description of Satan at once sublime and horrible, since he is indeed the god of all that believe not and works in them with inconceivable energy; note that the blinding is more than veiling, reaching the eye of the understanding itself; and take the word for illumination in its proper sense, the reflection or propagation of light from those already enlightened to others.

Set out the objection in the mouth of the heretic, who asks what sort of God causes blindness and cites this very verse, that in whom the God of this world hath blinded the minds of them that believe not, lest the light of the Gospel should shine unto them. Then answer it by reading a little before: if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in them that are perishing — see that it is in them that are perishing that it is veiled, for it is not right to give the things which are holy unto the dogs. Press the counter-question: is it only the God of the older covenant who has blinded the minds of them that believe not? Did not Jesus himself say that for this cause he speaks to them in parables, that seeing they may not see? Was it from hating them that he wished them not to see, or because of their unworthiness, since it was their own eyes that they had closed? Then state the rule the whole answer turns upon: where there is wilful wickedness, there is also a withholding of grace, for to him that hath shall be given, but from him that hath not shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have.

debates.question: Who is the god of this world?

sides.position: Satan, beyond any doubt for one who judges rightly
Satan, so called not from any hand in making or governing the world but from his hold on the worst part of it
The devil, whom a world worshipping hate and falsehood has practically deified
Possibly the supreme God, who in judgment gave the unbelieving over to darkness; there is reluctance in giving the title to Satan
Satan certainly; some of the Fathers read it of the true God, and Clarke inclines that way, but the name is given here because the world actually serves him

debates.question: Why did the Fathers read it of God rather than Satan?

sides.position: Hilary was pressed by Arians, Chrysostom and Augustine by Manicheans; the heat of controversy made them refute rather than investigate
The dispute survives in the exchange where the heretic asks what sort of God causes blindness and is answered from the previous verse

debates.question: Is the veil the gospel's fault or the hearer's?

sides.position: Neither the message nor any purpose of God to conceal it; the failure lies elsewhere
Those on the way to perish, not Judaising teachers only; and the present participle does not exclude future change
The blindness of unbelievers detracts nothing from the clearness of the gospel, for the sun is not less resplendent because the blind do not see his light

outliers.note: Alone declines to give the title of God to Satan, holding that but for a rooted prejudice in favour of the common opinion the supreme Being might well be understood — the reading Calvin traces to the heat of the Arian and Manichean controversies, and the one Barnes names him for holding.

Alone explains the history of the rival reading rather than merely refuting it, tracing it through Hilary, Chrysostom and Augustine to the pressures of controversy and concluding that they were more concerned to refute opponents than to find the writer's meaning.

themes: if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost
the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not
the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God

5.pericope_label: For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.

schools.summary: Hear an answer to a charge, since he had been accused of being egotistic in his preaching, perhaps with reference to particular passages of the earlier letter, and the repudiation is indignant: Christ Jesus had been the subject all along, and so far as he had spoken of himself at all it was as a servant for their sake. Add the blunt judgment that a preacher could find no poorer or more disgusting topic than himself, and that being your bond-slave for the sake of Jesus is sufficient reason for any preacher's sacrifice. Set the next verse in direct antithesis to the one before it — the god of this world did his work of blinding, the true God called light out of darkness — and note that the verb refers to a definite past fact, the moment of conversion, rather than a continuing state. Make the image domestic: a lamp lit in the heart, where miners carry theirs on the forehead. Say what the doctrines were not: not elaborated by human reasoning or science, nor imparted by tradition, but communicated directly by the source of all light. On the treasure, supply the custom behind it, that eastern kings stored their gold and silver in jars of earthenware, and hear a side glance at the taunts thrown out about the writer's bodily infirmities — be it so, he says, and let it appear that the excellence of the power is God's and not ours. Take the adjective back to its root, baked clay, the material of the inscribed fragments turned up in Egypt, and note the observation that the power is limitless but is stored in very unlikely receptacles. State the purpose without softening it: God, not man, is the dynamo, and the power comes from him and does not originate with us.

Give the reason for the disclaimer: the writer preached no doctrine of his own devising, set himself up as no lord over the faith and consciences of men, sought neither to display learning and eloquence nor to amass wealth, and did not assert the purity of human nature, the power of man to do spiritual good of himself, or a justification by works — all of which the false apostles did, and each of which is a way of preaching oneself. Report the proposal to read the sentence as a compressed antithesis, we preach not ourselves to be lords but God's only Son to be the one Lord, and while not finding fault with it prefer the plainer and more extensive sense, since men preach themselves in other ways than by arrogating dominion: by aiming at show rather than at edification, by desiring distinction in any form, by making gain of the work. On the light, canvass four ways of taking the clause. Two are subtleties that will not answer to the writer's intention, whether that God brought the light of the gospel into the world by the ministry of men who are in themselves darkness, or that he made the light of the gospel take the place of a law wrapt up in shadows. A third is the plain declaration that when all things were involved in darkness God kindled the light of his gospel. Prefer the fourth, which finds an allusion to the creation, so that he who by his word drew light out of the depth of darkness has now enlightened us spiritually when we were buried in darkness; the transition from light that is visible and corporeal to what is spiritual has more of elegance and there is nothing forced in it. Then turn the meanness of the vessel into the argument. Those who heard him glorying in such a strain and saw a person contemptible in the world's eyes might think him ridiculous; and what he saw to be most damaging to the honour of his apostleship among the ignorant he turns by an admirable contrivance into a means of advancing it, since treasure is not usually laid up in a splendid and elegantly adorned chest but rather in some mean and worthless one.

Take the three names in turn and say what each proclaims. Christ is the Anointed One of whom the prophets wrote, the expectation and the glory of Israel; Jesus is the Saviour and Deliverer who saves men from their sins, and it is Jesus of Nazareth who is declared to be that long-expected Messiah and no other; Lord is the great Ruler who has all power in heaven and earth, who made and governs the world and can save to the uttermost. Gloss the last clause by the standard of service it sets, labouring as fervently and faithfully for their eternal interests as a trusty slave does for his master's secular welfare, and doing it for Christ's sake and not for honour, interest or pleasure. On the light, argue from the parallel that the gospel is no human invention: as sure as God is the author of light and the creator of the universe, so sure is he the author of this, which is as far beyond man's wisdom and might as the creation of the world is beyond all created power. Take the purpose of the illumination to be transmission, that we might be given light in order to enlighten others. On the vessel, note that the word means more properly a vessel made of shells, which are very brittle, the shell being the outward part of a fish and so a fit resemblance of the body in which the soul dwells — recalling the philosophers who gave a man two bodies and called the one the chariot of the soul; and distinguish clay that has been through the kiln from clay that has not, the fired vessel being past mending once broken. Then apply the whole: the treasure belongs not to the apostles only but to all true believers, and afflictions and death itself, so far from hindering the ministration of the Spirit, further it, sharpen the ministers and increase the fruit.

Turn the verse into an argument from the preacher himself. Would you know that the Apostles knew and preached the name of Christ, or rather had Christ himself within them? He says to his hearers, Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me; and he proclaims Christ, saying that we preach not ourselves but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. Then ask who this is who says it, and answer: the former persecutor. Call it a mighty wonder that the persecutor himself preaches Christ, and press the question of what could account for it. Was he bribed? There was nobody to use that mode of persuasion. Was it that he saw him present on earth and was abashed? He had already been taken up into heaven. He went forth to persecute, and after three days the persecutor is a preacher in Damascus — by what power? Then set the evidence in order: others call friends as witnesses for friends, but here the witness produced is the former enemy. The testimony of Peter and John, though weighty, was of a kind open to suspicion, for they were his friends; but of one who was formerly his enemy, and afterwards died for his sake, who can any longer doubt the truth?

debates.question: What does it mean not to preach oneself?

sides.position: Not devising one's own doctrine, lording it over consciences, displaying learning, or teaching salvation by works
Not only refusing dominion but refusing display, distinction and gain
Surely as poor and disgusting a topic as a preacher can find
He was charged with being egotistic in his preaching and repudiates it indignantly

debates.question: What does the light out of darkness refer to?

sides.position: The creation, the transition from visible light to spiritual having elegance and nothing forced in it
The creation, so that the author of light is as certainly the author of the gospel, which is therefore no human invention
A definite past moment, the conversion itself, in direct antithesis to the blinding of the previous verse
A lamp lit within, where miners carry theirs on the forehead
A jar of the kind eastern kings kept treasure in, with a side glance at taunts about bodily weakness
A vessel of shell, brittle as the outer part of a fish; and fired clay is past mending once broken
A mean container deliberately chosen, so that what damaged his standing is turned into the argument for it
Baked clay, the material of the inscribed fragments found in Egypt; God, not man, is the dynamo

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into an evidential argument, contrasting the suspect testimony of friends with that of the former persecutor who afterwards died for the man he had hunted.
Alone canvasses four separate expositions of the light out of darkness and rejects two of them by name as subtleties that do not answer to the writer's intention.

themes: we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord
God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness

8.pericope_label: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body. For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. So then death worketh in us, but life in you.

schools.summary: Present the four clauses as participles in apposition with the subject of the preceding verse, and modify the English at each point to keep the antithesis: hemmed in in everything yet not straitened for room, perplexed yet not baffled, or, less literally but with more vividness, bewildered but not benighted. Take the imagery from the soldier on active service, pursued yet not abandoned, struck down as by a dart or javelin yet not perishing, and compare the faint yet pursuing of an old narrative of actual warfare — while allowing that the first verb may be traced to the pressing of grapes, and the third to the contests of wrestlers or of gladiators. Catch the play in the last pair, lost but not lost out, and ask whether the stoning at Lystra was in view. Then handle the dying of Jesus, and refuse the common reading of it. The word means deadness, the state of a corpse; it describes, by a bold hyperbole, the condition of one whose life was one long conflict with disease, dying daily, carrying in himself the very symptoms of death, dragging about with him what it was scarcely an exaggeration to call a living corpse. Say plainly that the words are often interpreted, but wrongly, of the dangers and sufferings caused by persecution, since the whole tenor of the letter suggests rather the daily struggle with pain and weakness; and answer the objection from the phrase for Jesus' sake by observing that a man who laboured as this man laboured, in a daily struggle with death and still working for the gospel, might well describe himself as bearing what he bore for that reason. On the closing antithesis, take life in its higher spiritual sense and trace the pathos of the earlier letter in the words — but note that the irony perceptible there is absent here.

Insist that the trouble is external, and argue it from the word, which signifies a thing dashed against from without: as the beating of the waves against a rock makes no trouble in the rock and no commotion there, but a great deal of noise and tumult round about it, so is the trouble meant here. Take the second term as a straitening that infers a difficulty of drawing breath, a man so compressed that he cannot tell how to breathe, so that the denial means we are not reduced to that extremity by all the troubles that surround us, but can breathe well enough for all that. Show what the abject condition is doing in the argument: so far from detracting from the glory of God, it is the occasion of advancing it, for we are reduced to straits and the Lord at length opens an outlet. Widen the first phrase three ways, taking it of every place, since wherever we go we are in the world and must expect tribulation; of every hour, since we are never free from one trial or another; and of every sort of person, good and bad, professors and profane, open persecutors and false brethren, since even weak believers among the children of God give trouble. Then read the closing sentence as irony, since it was unseemly that the Corinthians should live happily and at their ease, free from anxiety, while their teacher struggled with incessant hardships; such an allotment would have been exceedingly unreasonable, and their folly needed reproof, inasmuch as they had contrived for themselves a Christianity without the cross and, not content with that, held the servants of Christ in contempt for not being as effeminate as they.

Refer the four antitheses to the public games celebrated every fifth year near Corinth, and say that the terms cannot be understood except by reference to those exercises. Divide them: three of the four pairs belong to wrestling and the fourth to the footrace. The first verb belongs clearly to wrestling, since the man who can gripe his adversary and take him up is a good wrestler; the word for persecuted belongs to the race, where one runner being foremost the others pursue and get up close behind him but cannot outstrip him, which is what the denial means; and the word for cast down belongs to wrestling again, where he who throws the other first is the conqueror, so that not being destroyed means that though thrown down into troubles and difficulties they rose again and surmounted them. Distribute the eight terms differently as well: the four in the first verse respect inward afflictions and the four in the next outward, and in each clause the former part shows the earthen vessel while the latter shows the excellence of the power. On the bearing about of the dying, take it of being every moment in danger of losing life in the cause of truth, bearing the cross and ready to offer up life; and note that there is probably an allusion to the marks, wounds and bruises which contenders in those games got and carried throughout life. Take the manifesting of the life as the demonstration given by preservation, by the success of the ministry and by the works done. Close on the last clause plainly: the apostles are in continual danger and live a dying life, while those who received the gospel from them are in no such danger.

Give the account of their courage and patience clause by clause, and let each denial be answered by a reason. They were troubled on every side, afflicted many ways and meeting with almost all sorts of trouble, yet not distressed — not hedged in nor cooped up, because they could see help in God and help from God, and had liberty of access to him. They were perplexed, often uncertain what would become of them and not always without anxiety of mind on that account, yet not in despair, since even in their greatest perplexities they knew that God was able to support and to deliver, and placed their trust and hope in him. They were persecuted by men, pursued with hatred and violence from place to place as men not worthy to live, yet not forsaken of God — and note the distinction that carries the comfort, that good men may sometimes be forsaken of their friends, but not of him. Set the whole in its proper light: the apostles were great sufferers and in that followed their Master, who had told them that in the world they should have tribulation; yet they met with wonderful support, great relief, and many allays of their sorrows.

Show that the whole work is to be ascribed to the power of God, and by that means repress the highmindedness of those who glory in themselves. It is not only marvellous that this treasure is kept in earthen vessels, but that even while enduring ten thousand hardships and battered on every side they preserve it and do not lose it. Press the comparison: though there were a vessel of adamant, it would neither have been strong enough to carry so vast a treasure nor have sufficed against so many machinations; yet as it is, this one both bears it and suffers no harm, through God's grace. Then take the phrase on every side and unfold it — in respect of foes and in respect of friends, in respect of necessaries and of other needs, by those who are hostile and by those of our own household. And observe the method of the whole passage, how he speaks contraries on purpose, that from them also he may show the strength of God: pressed on every side yet not straitened, perplexed yet not unto despair. Explain the last denial exactly, that we do not quite fall off, for we are often wrong in our calculations and miss our aim, yet not so as to fall away from what is set before us, these things being permitted for our good.

debates.question: Where does the imagery of the four antitheses come from?

sides.position: The Isthmian games — three pairs from wrestling and one from the footrace
The soldier on active service, pursued yet not abandoned, struck down as by a javelin
Perhaps the contests of wrestlers or of gladiators
The first verb is the pressing of grapes; the last pair is lost, but not lost out

debates.question: Is the pressure inward or outward?

sides.position: The first four terms are inward and the next four outward
External: the word means a thing dashed against from without, as waves on a rock
Every place, every hour, and every sort of person, including weak believers

debates.question: What is the dying of Jesus that is carried about?

sides.position: Deadness, the state of a corpse: a life spent in conflict with disease, and the persecution reading is wrong
The marks of violence on the body, and the expectation of dying as his Master died
The wounds and bruises contenders carried through life
Perhaps the stoning at Lystra

outliers.note: Alone reads the dying of Jesus as a medical description — deadness, the state of a corpse, a life of conflict with disease — and says outright that the usual reference of the words to persecution is wrong.
Alone takes the closing antithesis as irony against readers who had contrived a Christianity without a cross, where Ellicott says expressly that the irony of the earlier letter is absent here.

themes: troubled on every side, yet not distressed
bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus
death worketh in us, but life in you

13.pericope_label: We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak; Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you. For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God.

schools.summary: Define the phrase carefully: the spirit of faith is not definitely the Holy Spirit, but the human spirit in fellowship with the Divine and therefore characterised by faith — or, more simply still, substantially the same as faith itself, a believing sense or impression of the truth. Note the formula introducing the citation, which occurs in legal documents in the papyri, and that the words are adapted rather than quoted exactly. Observe how apt the psalm's context is, since it speaks of the sorrows of death compassing the writer, of trouble and heaviness, of being brought low and delivered, as though that psalm had been his stay and comfort in his daily conflict; and deny that the psalmist had any reference to the preaching of the gospel. Draw a chronological inference from the next clause: the words about being presented together show that the writer was not certain he would be alive when Jesus comes, against what has been wrongly inferred from three passages of the earlier letter. On the resurrection, say clearly that what is in view is not deliverance from danger or disease but the resurrection treated at length before; prefer the reading of the better manuscripts, that we shall be raised with Jesus rather than by him, the received text having apparently arisen from a wish to adapt the words to the fact that Christ had already risen; and note that the verb rendered present is a favourite one for describing the work of Christ and the minister's own work. On the last verse, take the whole arrangement and its execution as designed to promote their salvation, and suspect a nearer motive as well, that stating it would conciliate the faction at Corinth. Then admit that the construction of the closing clause is obscure. The best sense is that grace, having abounded by means of the greater part of them, may cause thanksgiving to overflow to the glory of God; two other renderings are grammatically possible, which is more than can be said for the English version; and there is a play by which more is made through the more.

Take the faith here to be the grace and not the doctrine, a believing in the person of Christ and an expectation of the resurrection, together with a reliance on the power and promises of God to support under the afflictions of this life; and hold that the Spirit of God is the author of it, since it is not of ourselves nor of our own power but the free gift of God and the produce of his almighty power, which is why he is here called the Spirit of faith. Then settle whom the writer joins himself to. It has been thought that he speaks of the holy fathers under the older covenant and represents them as partakers with us in the same faith; that is true in itself, but it does not accord with the subject in hand, for it is not Abraham or the rest of the fathers whom he associates with himself here but the Corinthians — and the argument is that though God spares them and deals with them more indulgently while treating him more severely, the diversity is no hindrance to the like glorious resurrection awaiting both, since where there is oneness of faith there will be one inheritance. On the raising, refer it chiefly to the Father while denying that the Son and the Spirit were unconcerned in raising the body of Christ, and refuse to make Christ a mere instrument in the raising of the saints, since he is a co-efficient cause with the Father and the Spirit. Then read the last verse as the ground of a claim upon their sympathy: he associates himself with them not merely in the hope of future blessedness but in these very afflictions, letting them know that if he is afflicted it is for their benefit, so that there was good reason why they should transfer part of it to themselves. State the consolation in it — that while God, sparing our weakness, deals with us more gently, those endowed with more distinguished excellence are afflicted for the common advantage of all — and the duty that follows, that since they could not aid him otherwise they should at least help him by their prayers and sympathy.

Refer the spirit of faith to what animated the saints of old, and to David in particular when he said that he believed and therefore had spoken, meaning that he trusted in God and God put a song of praise in his mouth; and say what the corresponding speech is here, that we preach the gospel even in the midst of affliction and death because we believe that God will raise us up and present us with you. Being fully convinced of the truth of the Christian religion, we speak and testify that our deliverance is from God, and that he does not fail those who trust in him. On the resurrection, put the confidence at its strongest: though we shall at last seal this truth with our blood we do not fear, being persuaded that as the body of Christ was raised by the power of the Father so shall our bodies be raised, and that we shall have eternal life with him in glory. On the last verse, take all things to mean both the adverse and the prosperous, and read them as being for the profit of all who believe as well as all who preach: we proclaim these truths and bear these sufferings for your sakes, thinking all our sufferings nothing if we can gain converts to Christ and build believers up. Explain the closing clause as a wish that the gratitude of the multitudes converted may keep pace with the blessings they have received, and abound as those blessings have abounded; and add the reason it matters, that thanksgiving invites yet more abundant grace.

Say what the grace of faith does in a time of trouble: it is an effectual remedy against fainting. They knew that Christ was raised, and that his resurrection was an earnest and assurance of their own; and the hope of that resurrection will encourage in a suffering day and set a man above the fear of death. Add the second support, that their sufferings were for the advantage of the church and to God's glory, since the sufferings of Christ's ministers, as well as their preaching and their conversation, are for the good of the church and the glory of God. Then name the third, the prospect of eternal life and happiness, which was their support and comfort: what sense was ready to pronounce heavy and long, grievous and tedious, faith perceived to be light and short and but for a moment. Press the comparison home upon the reader — if the apostle could call his heavy and long-continued trials light and momentary, what must our trifling difficulties be? — and conclude that faith is what enables us to make this right judgment of things, since there are unseen things as well as things that are seen, and between them lies this vast difference, that the unseen are eternal.

debates.question: Is the spirit of faith the Holy Spirit?

sides.position: Yes: the faith is not of our own power but the gift and operation of God, and the Spirit is named from it
No: the phrase means substantially the same as faith itself
Neither exactly: the human spirit in fellowship with the Divine, and so characterised by faith

debates.question: Whose faith is called the same?

sides.position: The saints of old, and David in particular
Not Abraham or the fathers but the Corinthians; true in itself, but it does not fit the argument
The psalmist's, though he had no reference to the preaching of the gospel

debates.question: How should the closing clause be construed?

sides.position: That grace, having abounded through the greater part of you, may make thanksgiving overflow; two other renderings are possible, but not the English version's
That the gratitude of the converted may keep pace with the blessings received
More is made through the more

outliers.note: Alone draws a chronological conclusion from the clause about being presented together, holding that it shows the writer was not certain of surviving to the return of Christ, against inferences drawn from the earlier letter.
Alone makes the spirit of faith the Holy Spirit himself, on the ground that the faith in question is God's gift and operation rather than any power of ours.

themes: I believed, and therefore have I spoken
he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also
all things are for your sakes

16.pericope_label: For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory; While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.

schools.summary: Note the return, after a long digression, to the assertion the chapter opened with, and the change of imagery that comes with the repetition. Take the outward man to be the body, the material framework which is undergoing a gradual process of decay, and the inward man the higher spiritual life, passing day by day through successive stages of renewal and gaining fresh energies; and observe that by using the two phrases the writer shows he believed man to be made of two parts so distinct that while the one is enfeebled the other is strengthened, from which it follows that he was no materialist. Note also that the verb and its derivative are characteristic of this writer, that the same contrast of higher and lower nature appears elsewhere in his letters, that Plato has the phrase for the inward man, and that the expression for day by day occurs neither in the Greek version of the older Scriptures nor elsewhere here, being perhaps a colloquial repetition. On the sentence that follows, say that in energy and beauty of expression it is little inferior to anything in Demosthenes, that the writer's mind was labouring to convey ideas which language could very imperfectly communicate, and that the trials so described would to most people have seemed anything but light. Prefer the rendering the present lightness of our affliction as both more literal and better balanced; treat the doubled phrase as adverbial rather than adjectival, an intensity expressed after the Hebrew manner by repeating the same word; and set out the careful balancing of the terms, affliction against glory, lightness against weight, the moment against the eternal. On the last verse, gloss the participle as the contemplation of a goal one is striving towards, identify the things not seen with the objects of faith, and set beside them a sentence from a contemporary moralist, that what most men seek are but objects of imagination presenting a show of being for a time, so that the mind should be given to the things which are eternal.

Mark the rise in tone, as of a man who has carried his point: there is no cause why we should lose heart or sink under the burden of the cross, the issue of which is not merely desirable for ourselves but salutary for others. Turn that into an exhortation by example, that the Corinthians should be fortified should they be similarly afflicted, and into a rebuke of the fault they had erred in, since under the influence of ambition they held a man in higher estimation the further he stood from the cross of Christ. Then explain why the comparison is needed at all. Our flesh always shrinks back from its own destruction whatever reward is presented to our view, and we are influenced much more by present feeling than by the hope of heavenly blessings; so we are told that the afflictions of the pious have little or nothing of bitterness if compared with the boundless blessings of everlasting glory. Say why patience is so difficult a matter, that we are confounded on having experience of evils for a brief period; and since the outward is visible while the inward is not, the comparison between present misery and future felicity is drawn precisely to shake us off from a carnal attachment to the present life. On the last verse, name the thing that makes all the miseries of this world easy to be endured, namely carrying forward our thoughts to the eternity of the heavenly kingdom: a moment is long if we look around us on this side and on that, but when once we have raised our minds heavenward a thousand years begin to appear like a moment. Add what the words intimate, that we are imposed upon by the view of present things, so that there is nothing for us to rest upon but confidence in a future life; and give the verb its force, a steady intuition of the mark a man is aiming at, which he must always keep in his eye.

Return to the textual variant raised at the chapter's opening, since the same two readings stand here and are supported by much the same manuscripts; note that the editor who preferred the rarer reading at the first verse follows the common one here, though the variant is at least as well supported; and judge that the common reading, we faint not, agrees best with the writer's meaning. Take the outward man as the part that can be seen and heard and felt, slowly consumed by continual trials and martyred at last, and the inward as the soul, which cannot be seen by others and is revived and receives a daily increase of light and life from God, so that we grow more holy and more meet for glory every day; and report the Jewish opinion that even spirits stand in need of continual renovation, God renewing the angels daily by putting them into the fiery river from which they proceeded. On the sentence that follows, pass on the judgment that it is among the most emphatic passages in all these writings, the author speaking as much like an orator as like an apostle: the lightness claimed is levity itself in such a comparison, and the doubled phrase is infinitely emphatic and cannot be fully expressed by any translation, since all hyperboles fall short of describing that weight, and one may pass from hyperbole to hyperbole and still, at the last, be infinitely below it. Add the point that shows the writer's first language working in his second, that the Hebrew word for heavy also means glorious, and that the two significations are here united in a weight of glory; and say that the beauty and sublimity of the expressions surpass all imagination and can be preserved in no translation or paraphrase, every one of which must sink infinitely below the original. On the last verse, render the participle as aiming rather than looking, and state the limit exactly: the light afflictions work out this weight of glory only for those who do not look at the things which are seen, since a man may be grievously afflicted and yet have his eye bent on temporal good, and from his afflictions derive no benefit at all.

debates.question: Does the text here read we faint not or we act not wickedly?

sides.position: The same variant stands here, and the editor who preferred the rarer reading at verse one takes the common one here; the common reading suits the sense
The clause simply repeats the opening of the chapter

debates.question: What do the outward and inward man show about the writer?

sides.position: That he held man to be made of two parts so distinct that one decays while the other is renewed — he was no materialist
That the decay of the bodily organism is set against a growth in grace
Simply the body and the soul

debates.question: What are the things which are seen?

sides.position: The riches, honours and pleasures of this world
Possibly the afflictions themselves, equally open to the senses and equally temporary
All the incidents and circumstances of the present life, against the objects of faith

outliers.note: Alone returns to the textual variant he raised at the chapter's opening, and points out that the editor who preferred the rarer reading there takes the common one here, though it is as well supported in both places.
Alone offers a second sense for the things which are seen, taking them of the afflictions themselves rather than of worldly goods, so that a believer is not to stand poring over his own troubles.

a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory
the things which are not seen are eternal
